models.name: Designed for greater capability, faster inference, higher throughput, and scaling to larger models.
models.description: Readme DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is an advanced tool designed to enhance search capabilities, providing users with faster and more accurate results. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 552B backbone parameters and support for contexts of up to one million tokens. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses a Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED) design, stacking a 20-layer causal encoder on top of a 20-layer decoder for 40 Transformer layers total. Under CED, the decoder’s global KV cache is built by projecting the encoder’s final hidden states, instead of being computed from each decoder layer’s hidden states as it normally would be. As a result, only 8B parameters are active per token during prefill and 16B during decode , which cuts costs significantly for agentic workloads that process a lot of input. ￼ DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash builds on Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2) , where every attention layer runs in one of three fixed modes - Full , Reindex , or Reuse - letting layers share main KV, share indexer K, and recycle Top-K sparse-attention indices. In the decoder, a Hierarchical Sparse Indexer caps later indexing layers to a candidate pool built by the first Full Mode layer, so indexer cost at deeper layers stays bounded no matter how long the context gets. Together with FP4 main KV caching (E2M1 values, one E4M3 scale per 16 channels), this brings the global KV cache down to 890 bytes per token - about a quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash. GLM-5.3-Flash is the first natively multimodal model in Z.ai’s GLM-5 series. With 320B total parameters and just 18B active, it outperforms GLM-5.2 across benchmarks and real-world workloads at one-tenth the cost, while approaching Claude Opus 4.8 on coding and agentic benchmarks. Before release, Z.ai tested GLM-5.3-Flash anonymously as ox-alpha where it became the most popular model of the week. Flexible Thinking : Reasoning is always on, with effort tunable per request across low, high, and max levels. Multimodal Input : Accepts image and video alongside text, for workflows that mix code with visual context. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.1.1, it pushes the Pareto frontier at 57 points, a level of intelligence previously only available at roughly 10× the cost per task. Built for efficient inference GLM-5.3-Flash starts from a newly trained base model, with its architecture and training recipe redesigned around capability and efficiency. models.description: Readme Beam is an open model built by Reflection. Beam takes text as input and generates text as output. Beam uses a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 501B total parameters and 23B active parameters. It supports a context window of 1M tokens and was developed predominantly for English. Primary capabilities Token-efficient reasoning: Reaches comparable solution quality to leading open models using approximately 3x fewer inference-time reasoning tokens. Software engineering: Resolves real-world GitHub issues, operates in CLI and DevOps environments, and integrates directly with agentic coding harnesses. Code generation supported across languages. Agentic tool use: Long-horizon task completion, MCP-based tool integration, and browsing. Executes multi-step workflows from natural-language instructions. Reasoning (math and science): Graduate-level science problem solving, theorem proving, and applied mathematics. Reasoning quality transfers to debugging, planning, and self-correction during agentic execution. Model Overview Beam models are designed to deliver strong performance for areas such as agentic tool use, coding and general reasoning with an emphasis on token efficient usage. models.description: Readme d3 is a family of decision models from vLLM Semantic Router . Give it text, structured state, or a still image, then ask it to choose a category, answer yes or no, or rate something on a scale. It returns scores and probabilities for the options you provide. It does not write a conversational answer. Use d3 to route support requests, triage documents, prioritize cases, or check whether an image meets a criterion. You can ask several questions about the same input in one request. Get started d3 runs the 4B model, a good starting point on a 16 GB machine. This example routes a support request: ollama run d3 "A customer says their card was charged twice." \ --ask "Which team should handle this?" \ --choice 'billing=Invoices and charges' \ --choice 'returns=Refunds and replacements' \ --choice 'technical=App errors' d3 requires Ollama 0.40.9 or later. models.name: LFM3-VL-2B is a vision-language model for on-device visual understanding.
models.description: Readme LFM3-VL-2B is a vision-language model for on-device visual understanding. It takes text, images, and video (soon) as input, and combines the LFM3 language model with a new in-house vision encoder. New in LFM3-VL-2B: Video understanding (soon): the first LFM vision model that takes video as input. Ask questions about a recorded lecture, a walkthrough filmed on your phone, or a clip from a camera feed. Thinking: the model reasons step by step before it answers. This helps most with harder visual questions, such as math, charts, and multi-step problems. Spatial and embodied reasoning: the model finds objects and reasons about how they are placed relative to each other, a strong foundation for robotics applications. Model details The LFM3 family includes base, text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models. Property Specification Checkpoint Post-trained vision-language model Parameters 1.92B: 1.73B language model, 164M vision encoder, 25M projector Architecture LFM3, 24 layers: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention, 6 global attention Vision encoder 14 layers: 8 gated depthwise 2D convolutions, 6 bidirectional attention, 16×16 patches with 2D rotary embeddings Inputs Text, images, and video (soon) at native resolution. Each 2×2 block of patches becomes one language token. Video is sampled at 2 fps. Context length 128K tokens (input + output) Vocabulary 128,000 tokens Languages English, Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Hindi, Russian, Polish License LFM Open License v1.0 LFM3-VL-2B is designed for on-device visual tasks: questions about video, reading documents, charts, and app screens, finding objects in an image, and spatial reasoning for robots. It is not recommended for coding, multi-turn conversations, or complex reasoning. models.name: LFM3-Audio-2B is a compact, fully featured audio model.
models.description: Readme LFM3-Audio-2B is a compact, fully featured audio model that runs locally on laptops and edge devices. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both. Voice chat: ask questions aloud and receive streaming replies in text and speech. For text-only responses, the model can reason before answering. Multilingual speech: transcribe, synthesize, and translate speech across 18 languages. Audio understanding and reasoning: interpret recordings and answer questions about the speech, sounds, and events they contain. Tool calling: turn spoken requests into tool calls to control apps and devices, with text or speech alongside the calls. LFM3-Audio-2B introduces an in-house audio encoder and LiquidCodec audio tokenizer, improving speech quality over LFM2.5-Audio. Model details The LFM3 family includes base, text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models. Property Specification Parameters 2B total Architecture LFM3 backbone, causal audio encoder, and LiquidCodec audio tokenizer Input Text or audio; audio encoder operates at 16 kHz Output Text, 24 kHz speech, or interleaved text and speech Context length 32K tokens (input + output) Streaming Causal audio encoding, incremental prefill, and streaming speech generation Speech languages / locales Arabic, Danish, German, Greek, British English, American English, Finnish, French, Hebrew, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish, Chinese License LFM Open License v1.0 LFM3-Audio-2B is designed for local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, and domain-specific fine-tuning. Use retrieval or search for knowledge-heavy tasks. It is not recommended for agentic coding or complex multi-step reasoning due to its small size. models.name: pplx-decider-flash is a 4B decision model from Perplexity, built on Qwen3.5-4B
models.description: Readme pplx-decider-flash is a 4B decision model from Perplexity, built on Qwen3.5-4B and distilled from the pplx-decider models: the same request format and the same text and image support, at about one seventh of the size. Give it a state (text, JSON, or images) and a set of typed questions, and it returns a calibrated probability for every answer in a single forward pass. It doesn’t generate text. It’s compatible with the Jev and System One APIs, so it works through Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint and ollama run --ask . ollama pull pplx-decider-flash Highlights Most of the accuracy, a fraction of the size : Perplexity’s evaluation puts it at 58.88 overall on the Decision Index 0.3 (60.05 with one question per request) and 72.53 on the vision suite, against 68.09 and 77.43 for pplx-decider. Built for latency : Perplexity positions it for cases where latency or cost matters more than the last points of accuracy. Multimodal : decide over text, JSON, or images such as screenshots, receipts, and forms. One forward pass : every option of every question is scored together, with no output tokens. Apache 2.0 license What you can build Task You define You get back Route a request The destinations and when each applies The chosen destination and each destination’s probability Check a condition A yes or no question True or false, and the probability of each Grade an answer A rubric of levels The probability-weighted level and each level’s probability Gate an agent step A condition and the agent’s proposed action Go or no-go, with the probability of each CLI ollama run pplx-decider-flash --ask "Is a refund being requested?" < ticket.txt ollama run pplx-decider-flash --ask "Which team should handle this?" \ --choice billing="Payments and refunds" \ --choice technical="Outages and errors" < ticket.txt ollama run pplx-decider-flash --ask "How urgent is this?" \ --level "Routine" \ --level "Soon" \ --level "Immediate" < ticket.txt The state can also follow the model name instead

models.name: Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model and our most capable 3T-class model to date, with a 1M-token context window and major gains in coding, 3D creation, financial research, and factual accuracy.
models.description: Readme Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model, and our most capable 3T-class model to date. Post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains, it is the first model in the K3.1 series. With a 1-million-token context window, Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers substantial improvements in coding, 3D creation, financial research, factual accuracy, and other agentic capabilities. Key Features Efficient Long-Context Architecture : Kimi K3.1 Pro keeps Kimi K3’s 2.8T-parameter MoE design, activating 16 of 896 experts (104B active parameters), and replaces full-attention layers with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention for more efficient long-context modeling. Long-Horizon Coding : Kimi K3.1 Pro sustains long engineering sessions, from quick fixes to full-project builds, with stronger game development and script-driven 3D modeling in tools like Blender, CAD software and Unity. Financial Research & Factual Accuracy : Kimi K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, research and business operations, with improved factual accuracy over Kimi K3. Native Multimodality & Long Context : Kimi K3.1 Pro understands text and images, and supports a 1-million-token context window. Open Frontier Weights : We release the full Kimi K3.1 Pro model weights under the Kimi K3.1 Pro License. models.name: AutoTrust’s decision models return choices, yes/no probabilities, and ratings for the questions you supply
models.description: Readme AutoTrust’s decision models return choices, yes/no probabilities, and ratings for the questions you supply. Use them to route requests, classify documents, or grade an answer against your own criteria. Decisions from your criteria: define the categories or six rating levels that matter to your workflow. Probabilities for every option: use the full distribution when deciding what to automate or send for review. Several questions, one input: ask about the same text or structured state in a single request. Try it Route a customer request to the right team: ollama run autotrust-jev "My card was charged twice for the same order. Please refund the duplicate charge." \ --ask "Which team should handle this request?" \ --choice "billing=Charges, payments, and refunds" \ --choice "shipping=Deliveries and tracking" \ --choice "technical=App errors and account access" autotrust-jev runs AutoTrust’s 9B text model. For decisions about images, choose autotrust-jev:27b-vl or autotrust-jev:35b . See the decision documentation for CLI options and the API. Publisher results AutoTrust reports these results for its 9B checkpoint on its held-out test_set_30k evaluation: Task Publisher result Yes/no AUROC, all evaluation rows 0.996 Rating mean absolute error, 0–5 scale 0.103 See AutoTrust’s evaluation for the target distributions, data sources, and methodology. Credits Published by AutoTrust: 9B , 27B-VL , and 35B . Released under Apache 2.0 .
